fixes.explanation: I see why you'd think so, because the kings and merchants really do weep over Babylon (Revelation 18:9-11). But John hears something very different in heaven. The voices there are shouting, “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God!” Two different crowds, and this one is shouting praise.

You caught it, friend. The kings and merchants weep and mourn over Babylon (Revelation 18:9-11), but that's a different crowd. The voices John hears in heaven are shouting, “Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God!” John says it sounds like the roar of a great multitude.

Not what the voices say, friend. The kings of the earth show up earlier in Revelation weeping over Babylon (Revelation 18:9), and nothing here says they made peace with anybody. The reason in heaven is this: “For His judgments are true and just.” I once spent a week sure my oven was broken when the pilot light was just off, so I know how easy it is to grab the nearest cause.

Not yet, baker, because the voices have more to say. Verse 3 says a second time they call out, “Hallelujah! Her smoke rises forever and ever.” So the first shout wasn't the whole thing. Heaven has another one coming.
Yes, baker. The twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down and worshiped God who sits on the throne. Then they said, “Amen, Hallelujah!” Down on the ground, and straight into praise.

Dust on the head shows up in the mourning over Babylon (Revelation 18:19), so it belongs to that scene. In this verse, the elders and the living creatures do something else. They fell down and worshiped God who sits on the throne, saying, “Amen, Hallelujah!”
That's it, friend. The voice from the throne says, “Praise our God, all you who serve Him, and those who fear Him, small and great alike!” Notice how wide that circle is, small and great alike.
Wise is a fine word, friend, but it isn't the one in the text. The voice says, “…small and great alike!” The call goes to the small and the great together.

Good thought, friend, but those aren't the words. The voices cry out, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.” That's their reason, right inside the shout. Gathering the nations isn't in it, and when a crowd sounds like many waters and thunder, I'd listen closely to every word.

Not in this verse, baker. Listen to what the multitude actually cries: “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns.” The reason is His reign, and it comes with a sound like rushing waters and thunder. I bet I'd have stood there with my mustache hanging open.

Not here, friend. The voices call out, “Let us rejoice and be glad and give Him the glory.” Then they give the reason: “For the marriage of the Lamb has come…” So what has come is a marriage, not a harvest.

That's not part of what they say, baker. They call out, “Let us rejoice and be glad and give Him the glory.” The news that follows is, “For the marriage of the Lamb has come…” There's no temple in these words, only the marriage of the Lamb.

The text doesn't say that, friend. The clothing is “bright and pure,” and the verse gives its own answer: “For the fine linen she wears is the righteous acts of the saints.” The linen stands for righteous acts, not for riches.

Seating isn't mentioned, friend. The angel says, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” The blessing is about being invited. Then he adds, “These are the true words of God.”

That isn't what the angel says, baker. John is told to write, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” The blessing goes to those who are invited. The angel says of those words, “These are the true words of God.”

No title like that, friend. When John falls at his feet, the angel says, “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who rely on the testimony of Jesus.” Then he tells John, “Worship God!” That's how he describes himself.

That isn't how he describes himself, baker. The angel says, “I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who rely on the testimony of Jesus.” He calls himself a servant with John and John's brothers. Then he points John to God: “Worship God!”
